# Feathers!

- An extant avian apomorphy (shared with some theropods)
- Mostly made from beta-keratin---strong protein polymer unique to birds and reptiles  

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.15\linewidth]{images/amazon_feather.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny ([Cornell](https://academy.allaboutbirds.org/feathers-article/))

# Feather anatomy

- An extant avian apomorphy (shared with some theropods)
- Mostly made from beta-keratin---strong protein polymer unique to birds and reptiles  

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = \linewidth]{images/feather_anatomy.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny ([Cornell](https://academy.allaboutbirds.org/feathers-article/))

# Feather types

- Wing (remige) and tail (retrix) help with flight, mobility, displays
- Contours cover body
- Down and semiplumes insulate, lack hooks on barbules; differ by presence of rachis in latter
- Bristles and filoplumes have sensory purposes

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.8\linewidth]{images/feather_types.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny ([Cornell](https://academy.allaboutbirds.org/feathers-article/))

# Powder down

- Found in herons, pigeons, doves, tinamous, bustards and some parrots
- Down feathers that never molt, grow continuously, and break down into a talcum-powder like substance at the tip

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.7\linewidth]{images/powderdown.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny ([BirdNote](https://www.birdnote.org/))

# Remiges

- Asymmetrical for flight
- Barbs have hooked barbules of central rami (ramus)
- Planar surface on either side of rachis called "vanes"

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.9\linewidth]{images/amazon_wing.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny ([Cornell](https://academy.allaboutbirds.org/feathers-article/))

# Remiges

- 9-12 primaries (attach to carpometacarupus)
- 6-40 secondaries (attach to ulna)

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.9\linewidth]{images/molt2.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Pyle 1997)

# Remiges

- 6 secondaries in hummingbirds
- 40 secondaries in albatross

# Retrices

- attach to pygostyle

# Modified retrices

- Sexual selection can modify retrices for display (birds of paradise)
- Natural selection can modify retrices for foraging niche (woodpeckers)

# Feather development: Stages

- Epidermis thickens to **placaode**, elongates into **feather germ**, invaginates to form **follice**, develops barbs and rachis inside **sheath** that sheds when growth is complete
- Complete feathers are dead stuctures!

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.9\linewidth]{images/feather_growth.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny ([Cornell](https://academy.allaboutbirds.org/feathers-article/))

# Feather tracts

- Feather tracts are called pterylae 
- Regions between tracts called apteria 

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.6\linewidth]{images/nutcracker_tracts.jpg}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Mewaldt 1958)

# Evo-devo feather development hypothesis

- Feather morphology evolution inferred by order of dependency of features during development (e.g., rachis is formed by fusion of barbs)

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.6\linewidth]{images/prum_figs.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Prum 1999)

# Feather coloration: pigments

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.9\linewidth]{images/pigments.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny ([Cornell](https://academy.allaboutbirds.org/how-birds-make-colorful-feathers/))

# Melanins

- Pigments responsible for browns and blacks
- Produced by melanosome organelles; transferred to feathers and retained in beta-keratin
- Makes feathers more durable and resistant to bacteria

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.7\linewidth]{images/ghow.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny ([*Bubo virginianus*](https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/55215981))

# Carotenoids

- Pigments responsible for reds, yellows, and oranges
- Obtained from dietary sources
- Can interact with melanins to create olive-green 

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.7\linewidth]{images/blackburnian.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny ([*Setophaga fusca*](https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/168328191))

# Porphyrins 

- Chemically similar to chlorophyll and heme (in hemoglobin)
- Browns and reds; degrade easily under light
- Creates short-lived color that may signal virginity in bustards!

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.7\linewidth]{images/galvan.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Galván et al. 2016)

# Psittacofulvins

- Pigments responsible for orange, yellow, and bright red in parrots
- Synthesized in feather cells; color variation from mutation impacting oxidation state

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.8\linewidth]{images/psittacofulvins.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Arbore et al. 2024)

# Feather coloration: structural color

- Blues; can combine with carotenoids to produce greens (except in Turacos; "turacoverdin")

\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny ([Cornell](https://academy.allaboutbirds.org/how-birds-make-colorful-feathers/))

# Feather care

- Preening with bill and feet: arrange barbs, remove parasites
- Waterproof with secretions from uropygial gland

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.6\linewidth]{images/uropygial.png} 
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uropygial_gland))

# Feather replacement: molt

- Birds replace old feather 2-3x during their first year; 1-2x / year after

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.6\linewidth]{images/molt_kurt.png} 
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny ([IBP](https://www.birdpop.org/pages/blogPost.php?id=27))

# Classic molt patterns

- One molt per year: chickadees, hawks, hummingbirds, jays, etc
- One complete / one partial molt per year: tanagers, warblers, buntings

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = \linewidth]{images/molt_cycles.png} 
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Gill et al. 2019; Dunn et al. 2017)

# This Orange-crowned Warbler bred in Glacier NP and is about to migrate to Mexico. What molt did it last undergo?

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.5\linewidth]{images/ocwa.png} 
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny ([*Leiothlypis celata*](https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/264994961)  

\normalsize

a) prealternate molt
b) prebasic molt
c) prejuvenal molt
d) first prebasic molt

# Centrifugal molt

- Many species (esp. passerines) begin with first primary and molt outwards towards p10

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.8\linewidth]{images/molt_gill.png} 
\end{figure}  
\hfill \tiny (Gill et al. 2019)


# Synchronous molt

- Waterfowl molt all primaries simultaneously, lose ability to fly for several weeks
- Males in basic plumage during this stage

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.8\linewidth]{images/mallard_molt.png} 
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny ([Marlin Harms](https://www.flickr.com/photos/marlinharms/28936254066))

# "Molt" by wear

- Plumage can also change by wear and abrasion, e.g. Snow Buntings

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = \linewidth]{images/bunting_wear.png} 
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny ([Birds of the World](https://birdsoftheworld.org/bow/species/snobun/cur/appearance#molts))
